blocks.text: A 66-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has a small cut on his heel that has not healed after eight weeks. A different patient develops a hard, raised, itchy scar on her earlobe that grows beyond the original piercing. A third, after twenty years of heavy drinking, has a liver that has become a nodular, shrunken scarred organ. Each is a failure of the normal balance of repair.

blocks.markdown: Normal healing depends on adequate blood supply, an absence of infection and foreign material, sufficient nutrients and a regulated balance between matrix deposition and degradation. Wound healing can fail in two opposite directions: **deficient healing** (delayed healing, wound dehiscence, chronic ulcers) and **excessive healing** (hypertrophic scars, keloids, organ fibrosis).

rows: Persistent inflammation; bacteria and neutrophil enzymes destroy tissue
Poor blood supply (arterial or venous disease)
Reduced oxygen, nutrients and cell delivery
Mechanical stress or poor apposition of edges
Impaired vascular supply, neuropathy, impaired leucocyte function and infection
Malnutrition; vitamin C deficiency; zinc deficiency
Impaired collagen synthesis and cross-linking (vitamin C is needed for hydroxylation of proline and lysine)
Suppress inflammation, fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis
Reduced proliferative response and oxygen delivery
blocks.caption: Local and systemic factors that delay wound healing.

blocks.title: Why is the diabetic ulcer not healing?
blocks.prompt: A patient with long-standing diabetes has a heel ulcer. List the local and systemic factors contributing to impaired healing.

steps.text: Systemic: hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function and fibroblast activity; microvascular and macrovascular disease reduce perfusion.
Local: peripheral neuropathy leads to unnoticed repeated pressure, causing mechanical trauma.
Local: reduced arterial supply produces hypoxia; the ulcer is prone to infection and necrotic tissue.
The result is persistent inflammation without progression to granulation tissue maturation: a chronic ulcer.

blocks.answer: Ischaemia, neuropathy and repeated pressure (local), with hyperglycaemia and impaired immune function (systemic), prevent healing.

blocks.title: Hypertrophic scar and keloid
blocks.text: A hypertrophic scar is excessive collagen that stays within the boundary of the original wound and often regresses. A keloid is an exuberant scar of disorganised thick collagen bundles that grows beyond the original wound margins onto normal skin, does not regress and recurs after excision.

blocks.markdown:
### Pathogenesis of excessive scarring

Both lesions result from excessive or prolonged fibroblast activity with insufficient matrix degradation. Persistent inflammation, wound tension and high levels of **TGF-beta** and other growth factors stimulate fibroblasts to produce excess type I and type III collagen. In keloids, there is an inherited tendency; they are more common in people with darker skin pigmentation, and occur typically on the earlobes, sternum and shoulders. Histologically, keloids show thick, glassy, hyalinised eosinophilic collagen bundles. Hypertrophic scars occur in wounds under tension or after burns and show collagen arranged in nodules oriented parallel to the surface.

rows: Extends beyond wound onto normal skin
Nodules of mostly type III collagen aligned with surface
blocks.caption: Hypertrophic scars compared with keloids.

blocks.markdown:
### Chronic injury and organ fibrosis

In the viscera, repetitive or persistent injury produces fibrosis instead of regeneration. The principle is the same as in skin: persistent injury and inflammation activate matrix-producing cells through cytokines (particularly TGF-beta), and the normal feedback that removes myofibroblasts fails. Collagen accumulates, parenchyma is replaced, architecture is distorted and function is lost.

**Cirrhosis** is the model. Chronic injury to hepatocytes (alcohol, hepatitis B or C virus, fatty liver disease) causes necrosis and inflammation. **Hepatic stellate cells** in the perisinusoidal space of Disse become activated into myofibroblasts under the influence of TGF-beta and PDGF from injured hepatocytes and Kupffer cells, and secrete type I and III collagen. Septa of fibrous tissue form, **regenerating nodules** of hepatocytes are surrounded by fibrous bands, and the normal lobular architecture is destroyed. The consequences are **portal hypertension** (from resistance to blood flow) and **hepatocellular failure**.

blocks.title: From alcohol to cirrhosis
blocks.prompt: Describe, in order, how 20 years of heavy alcohol intake can produce cirrhosis.

steps.text: Alcohol metabolites injure hepatocytes, causing fatty change, necrosis and inflammation (alcoholic hepatitis).
Kupffer cells and injured hepatocytes release TGF-beta and PDGF; stellate cells become myofibroblasts and deposit collagen.
Collagen bands link portal tracts and central veins; surviving hepatocytes regenerate as nodules but without normal architecture.
The distorted liver impedes portal blood flow, giving portal hypertension, and loses synthetic function.

blocks.answer: Chronic injury, stellate cell activation, collagen septa, nodular regeneration, then portal hypertension and liver failure.

items: Fibrosis is the endpoint of chronic injury in many organs: lung (pulmonary fibrosis), kidney, liver and heart.
Activated myofibroblasts are the main source of collagen; TGF-beta is the key signal.
Fibrosis can sometimes regress early if the cause is removed, but established cirrhosis is largely irreversible.
Wound dehiscence is separation of wound edges, and is more common after abdominal surgery with increased intra-abdominal pressure.

blocks.title: Two directions of failure
blocks.text: Healing may be too little (infection, ischaemia, diabetes, steroids, vitamin C deficiency) or too much (keloid, hypertrophic scar, organ fibrosis). The mediator common to excess scarring is TGF-beta.

points: Local factors (infection, ischaemia, foreign bodies, tension) and systemic factors (diabetes, malnutrition, steroids, vitamin C deficiency, age) delay healing.
Keloids extend beyond the wound margin and recur; hypertrophic scars stay within it and may regress; both reflect excess collagen deposition.
Chronic injury activates myofibroblasts and, in the liver, stellate cells to lay down collagen, producing cirrhosis with portal hypertension.

questions.stem: Which systemic factor impairs wound healing by suppressing inflammation and collagen synthesis?
questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids dampen inflammation and reduce fibroblast activity and collagen synthesis, delaying repair. The other options favour normal healing.

questions.stem: A sailor on a long voyage with a poor diet develops bleeding gums and old healed scars that re-open. Which mechanism best explains the failure of repair?

options.text: Vitamin C deficiency impairs hydroxylation of proline and lysine, so collagen is defective
Excess TGF-beta causes overproduction of collagen
Vitamin K deficiency prevents collagen synthesis

questions.correctOptionText: Vitamin C deficiency impairs hydroxylation of proline and lysine, so collagen is defective

distractorRationale.b: Excess TGF-beta causes fibrosis, not poor healing.
distractorRationale.d: Vitamin K deficiency affects clotting factors.

questions.explanation: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine in procollagen requires vitamin C, so scurvy produces weak collagen and defective healing. Excess scar formation would be the opposite problem.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a firm raised scar that has spread beyond the margins of an earlier ear piercing onto normal skin. Which feature would be expected on histology?

options.text: Thick, glassy, eosinophilic bundles of disorganised collagen

questions.correctOptionText: Thick, glassy, eosinophilic bundles of disorganised collagen

distractorRationale.d: Normal collagen would not give a keloid.

questions.explanation: A scar that extends beyond the original wound is a keloid, characterised by thick hyalinised collagen bundles. Keloids tend to recur after excision.

questions.stem: Which cell is the main source of collagen in the fibrotic liver of cirrhosis?

distractorRationale.b: Hepatocytes are injured cells that regenerate as nodules.
distractorRationale.c: Kupffer cells release cytokines but are not the main collagen source.

questions.explanation: Stellate cells in the space of Disse transform into myofibroblast-like cells and secrete collagen under TGF-beta. Kupffer cells and hepatocytes contribute signals.

questions.stem: True or false: A hypertrophic scar remains within the boundaries of the original wound, whereas a keloid extends beyond them.
questions.explanation: Confinement to the wound boundary is the defining difference. Keloids grow onto normal skin and recur after excision.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly describes consequences of cirrhosis?

options.text: Portal hypertension and loss of hepatocellular function
Hepatic regeneration to normal architecture and reduced portal pressure
Portal hypotension and increased synthetic function

questions.correctOptionText: Portal hypertension and loss of hepatocellular function

distractorRationale.c: Cirrhosis raises, not lowers, portal pressure.
distractorRationale.d: Granulomas are not the characteristic lesion.

questions.explanation: Fibrous septa and regenerating nodules distort blood flow, raising portal pressure, while the replacement of parenchyma impairs hepatic function.

questions.stem: On day 7 after a laparotomy in a 70-year-old obese man who is coughing heavily, the wound edges separate. Which local factor most directly explains this complication?

options.text: Mechanical stress on a wound whose tensile strength is still low

questions.correctOptionText: Mechanical stress on a wound whose tensile strength is still low

distractorRationale.a: Correct: dehiscence follows tension on a wound before it has gained strength.
distractorRationale.b: Keloid is excess scarring and takes longer to develop.
distractorRationale.c: Caseous necrosis is not part of this scenario.

questions.explanation: Raised intra-abdominal pressure from coughing and obesity stresses a wound that has only about 10% of its final strength at one week. Mechanical stress is a recognised local cause of delayed healing and dehiscence.

questions.stem: List four local and four systemic factors that delay wound healing and explain the mechanism for one of each.
markingGuide: Local: infection, poor blood supply, foreign body or necrotic tissue, mechanical stress/poor apposition (any four)
Systemic: diabetes, malnutrition/vitamin C or zinc deficiency, glucocorticoids, ageing, obesity, anaemia (any four)
Mechanism for a local factor, e.g. ischaemia reduces oxygen and nutrient delivery or infection prolongs inflammation
Mechanism for a systemic factor, e.g. vitamin C needed for collagen hydroxylation or steroids suppress fibroblasts
questions.explanation: Healing needs perfusion, absence of infection and nutrients, so local and systemic deficits in these delay repair. Linking each factor to its mechanism shows understanding.

questions.stem: Distinguish a keloid from a hypertrophic scar and describe the pathogenesis common to both.
markingGuide: Hypertrophic scar confined to wound margins and may regress; keloid extends beyond margins, persistent, recurs
Keloid: thick hyalinised disorganised collagen bundles; familial and ethnic predisposition
Common pathogenesis: excess fibroblast activity and collagen deposition relative to degradation
Role of TGF-beta and other growth factors, wound tension and persistent inflammation
questions.explanation: Both reflect an imbalance between collagen synthesis and degradation. The extent beyond the wound and the tendency to regress distinguish them.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C has developed a small, nodular liver with ascites. Explain how chronic injury has led to cirrhosis and why portal hypertension results.
markingGuide: Release of TGF-beta and PDGF activates hepatic stellate cells into myofibroblasts
Collagen deposition forms fibrous septa linking portal tracts and central veins
Regenerating hepatocyte nodules with loss of normal architecture
Distorted sinusoids and vascular architecture increase resistance to portal flow: portal hypertension (ascites)
Loss of functional parenchyma leads to hepatic failure
questions.explanation: Cirrhosis results from sustained injury that activates collagen-producing cells and distorts lobular architecture. The increased resistance to portal flow explains portal hypertension and ascites.
